newsitem.title: belgium: EU commission slams Renault over plant closure.
newsitem.headline: EU commission slams Renault over plant closure.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday that French car maker Renault had clearly breached European Union directives in its handling of plans to close its Belgian assembly plant.

After European Commissioners discussed the issue during their weekly meeting in Brussels, Commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said: "The conclusion is that Renault have not respected the directives."
Plans by Renault to close its factory in Vilvoorde have sparked outrage in Belgium, where prospects of re-employment for over 3,000 workers are slim.

The Commission -- the EU's executive -- stressed that it was powerless to take action against Renault over the closure, but implicitly suggested it was encouraging either the Belgian state or Renault workers to take legal action.
"Regardless of whether they did or did not follow directives, the spirit of the law was not respected," Santer said in a statement read earlier to reporters by Van der Pas.
Asked if this could be interpreted as support for legal action against Renault, he replied: "You can take that as encouragement."
Van der Pas told Reuters following the Commission meeting that the Commissioners felt Renault was clearly in breach of two EU directives related to factory closures.
One insists companies negotiate with workers before taking a final decision on closure and the other says public authorities must be notified in advance.
Both directives have become law in France and Belgium, but the Commission said it was up to a member state or the workers to press the issue in court.
"Without prejudice to anything the Belgian authorities may undertake, it is up to the workers or any other interested party to take the issue to national courts," Van der Pas said.
He said the commisioners debated whether Renault's breach of the directives came about because the guidelines were not specific enough or had not been properly enforced.
"They decided it seemed it was the latter," he said. "It is a case of non-enforcement."
Nevertheless, European social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn had been asked by Santer to re-examine EU directives on the implications of factory closures to see if they could be strengthened.

Van der Pas said Santer had also raised "on a general nature" the possibility of examining more closely whether companies were taking advantage of state or EU aid to relocate, only to move again once funds dried up.
He said, however, there was no suggestion Renault had used this tactic.
Earlier, Flynn's spokeswoman Barbara Nolan said questions still need to be answered about the whole affair.
"It seems the workers have been left with a fait accompli," she said. "There are serious questions that need to be answered by Renault, but it is up to national authorities to pursue them."
Santer discussed the issue with Belgium's King Albert II during a meeting earlier on Wednesday and Van der Pas said both men expressed concern for the fate of the workers who will lose their jobs.
The decision to close the plant has been met by outrage from Belgian authorities, the Flanders regional government and trade unions.

It has sparked calls for a Belgian boycott of Renault cars and prompted the government to cancel an order for 150 Renault vehicles. Other officials have threatened to bar the company from public procurement tenders.
Willy Helin, spokesman for European Competition commissioner Karel van Miert, said it looked as if Renault may have a case to answer.

"His (Van Miert's) analysis of the explanations from several sources has led him to believe that Renault may not have followed the correct procedure," Helin said. "Speaking as an individual, a Belgian and a commissioner, he has formed his opinion."
